1135.title: A lotus at every name
1135.hook: Vishnu offers Shiva a lotus for every name, and at the last name, the lotus is gone
1135.carry: every name an offering, even from vishnu to shiva
1135.howItsDone: Hindus tell this story of Vishnu's lotuses in the Shiva Purana, and in a Shiva temple a devotee may sponsor an archana in which a flower is offered at each of Shiva's names.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Last time, the Shiva Sahasranama brought Pashupati, lord of every creature, the one who loosens the rope. A new week, and a new story.
screen: `PASHUPATI LOOSENS THE ROPE.` · `A NEW WEEK, A NEW STORY.`

segments.voice: One lotus is missing. Vishnu has been kneeling before Shiva for a long time, saying a name and laying down a lotus, a name and a lotus, over and over. There should be a flower for every name. Now, with one name left to say, his hand reaches into the basket and finds nothing. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it, and it's how that Purana frames its own list of Shiva's names.
screen: `A NAME, A LOTUS.` → `ONE NAME LEFT.` → `THE BASKET IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana, Vishnu needs Shiva's help. The demons are winning, so Vishnu goes to Shiva's shrine to honor him with a thousand names, a lotus at each one. Shiva decides to test him, and quietly hides one lotus. So: the empty basket. What does Vishnu do? Instead he remembers what people call him: Kamala-nayana, the lotus-eyed. His eyes are lotuses, he thinks, so he means to offer one of them. As he reaches to take out his own eye, Shiva appears and stops him, delighted, and gives him a gift: the Sudarshana, the blazing discus Vishnu carries from then on. Hindus keep this story for two reasons. First, it shows what a name is for. In Hindu worship, saying God's name is itself an offering. In an archana at a temple, the priest says a name and lays down a flower, a name and a flower, the way Vishnu did. Each name was a gift, so when the flowers ran out, Vishnu gave himself. Second, look at who's kneeling. Vishnu, the great god of one huge family of Hindus, worshipping Shiva, the great god of another, with no one shamed. Many teachers read stories like this as a quiet warning against turning the gods into rival teams. Plenty of Hindu homes keep both on one shelf, and some temples show them as one figure, half Vishnu and half Shiva: Harihara. So if your family's shelf is all Krishna and your grandmother goes to Shiva's temple on Mondays, nobody is switching sides. Vishnu got there first.
screen: `VISHNU: A NAME AND A LOTUS EACH.` · `SHIVA HIDES ONE LOTUS.` · `THE LOTUS-EYED OFFERS HIS EYE.` · `A NAME IS AN OFFERING.` · then, large: `NOT RIVAL TEAMS.`

segments.voice: Pick a name of God you love, Shiva, Krishna, the Goddess, or simply God, and say it silently once on each out-breath, as if you were laying down a flower each time. When your mind wanders, that's your empty basket: just come back and give the next name, the latest as real as the first. If you don't pray, offer one thing you're grateful for on each breath instead.

1136.title: Nilakantha, the blue throat
1136.hook: Nilakantha, the blue-throated: why Shiva drank the poison, and why devotees pour cool water over him
1136.carry: shiva held the poison so the world wouldn't burn
1136.tomorrow: why would anyone bow to God's anger?
1136.howItsDone: Hindus tell the churning of the ocean in the Mahabharata and the Puranas; devotees honor Shiva as Nilakantha and pour water or milk over the Shiva linga in abhisheka, which many say cools the poison in his throat, especially in the month of Shravan.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Sahasranama, Vishnu laid a lotus at every name, and offered his own eye when one went missing. Today, a name with a scar.
screen: `A LOTUS AT EVERY NAME.` · `A NAME WITH A SCAR.`

segments.voice: In paintings and posters of Shiva, look at his throat. It's blue. The throat carries a darker stain, like a bruise. Some of his names describe how he looks or what he rules. This one remembers something he did, and marks the place on his body where it happened: Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.
screen: `LOOK AT HIS THROAT.` → `A NAME THAT REMEMBERS.` → `NILAKANTHA.`

segments.voice: Nila is blue, a dark blue-black, and kantha is the throat. The story behind it is the churning of the ocean, told in the Mahabharata and the Puranas. The gods and the demons want amrita, the nectar of immortality, and it lies at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they make a churn out of a mountain, use the great serpent as the rope, and pull, the gods at one end and the demons at the other. Treasures rise, and then something terrible: a poison, halahala, so strong it begins to burn the worlds. Nobody wants it. The gods and the demons both turn to Shiva. And Shiva drinks it. In some tellings Parvati puts her hand to his throat so it won't go down; in others his own power holds it there. Either way, the poison stops at the throat and stains it blue. So the name is a scar, worn openly. Here's the teaching Hindus act out with their hands. Shiva is the God who takes in what would destroy everyone else. And devotees answer with care. When they pour water or milk over the Shiva linga, the ritual bath called abhisheka, many families say it's to cool him, because the poison is still in his throat. In the monsoon month of Shravan, which many say is when the churning happened, crowds of pilgrims carry river water for miles to pour over him. Some teachers add a reading for family life: someone often holds the hard news so it doesn't spread, and the cool water is how you thank them.
screen: `NILA, KANTHA: BLUE, THROAT.` · `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `SHIVA DRINKS THE POISON.` · `ABHISHEKA: WATER TO COOL HIM.` · then, large: `HE HELD IT FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: If you can, hold a glass of water. Breathe slowly through the throat, cool on the way in, warm on the way out. Let one hard thing from this week come to mind, a sharp word you heard or nearly said, and let it rest at the throat for a breath or two, not pushed down and not thrown back. Then take a slow sip, the way devotees pour cool water for Nilakantha. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya softly; if you don't, just notice the cool.

1137.title: The fierce one who heals
1137.hook: a Vedic poet bows to the fierce, braided-haired god, and asks him to heal
1137.carry: rudra the fierce is shiva, the kind
1137.tomorrow: what did a poor boy want more than milk?
1137.howItsDone: Images of Shiva keep his coiled, matted hair, and the Shri Rudram, the Vedic litany that opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, is chanted as water and milk are poured over the Shiva linga.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Shiva Sahasranama gave Nilakantha: the blue throat that held the poison. Today, the braided hair.
screen: `NILAKANTHA, THE BLUE THROAT.` · `THE BRAIDED HAIR.`

segments.voice: A prayer for a village can be very practical. Keep the children well. Keep the animals healthy. Let nobody fall sick. In the Rig Veda, a poet brings exactly that kind of prayer to Rudra, the fierce god whose names Shiva carries. And before he asks for anything, he names him: strong, and kapardin, the one with braided, coiled hair. This is a god people were afraid of. So why go to him for medicine?
screen: `A PRAYER FOR A VILLAGE.` → `KAPARDIN, THE BRAIDED HAIR.` → `WHY ASK THE FIERCE ONE?`

segments.voice: Kaparda is a braid or coil of hair, and kapardin is the one who wears it, the same piled locks you still see on Shiva today. In the Rig Veda, Rudra is the fierce one, a god of the wild places, with arrows people pray will miss them. In this very hymn the poet begs him: don't harm our children, our cattle, our people; don't strike in anger. And yet the same hymn pictures him holding healing medicines in his hand, and another hymn calls him the greatest healer of all healers. The village doesn't run from the frightening god. It bows to him, by name, and asks for the gentle side of the same power. Out of that grows one of the oldest teachings about Shiva. The word shiva first meant kind, auspicious, gracious, and the Vedic poets prayed for Rudra's shiva form, his kind form. Over time, scholars and teachers note, the hope became the name. The fierce one is the kind one. Hindu worship doesn't split God into a good god and a scary one. The Shri Rudram, a Vedic litany of Rudra's names still chanted when water is poured over the Shiva linga, opens by bowing to his anger and his arrow, and asks that they turn kind. Many teachers read it as a way to pray with your fear, not around it: name the frightening thing, bow, and ask for grace. Families still have the Rudram chanted for health and for blessings on a home. A village asking to be well, all over again.
screen: `KAPARDA: COILED, BRAIDED HAIR.` · `HIS ARROWS FEARED, HIS MEDICINES IN HAND.` · `SHIVA: KIND, AUSPICIOUS.` · `THE RUDRAM BOWS TO HIS ANGER.` · then, large: `THE FIERCE ONE IS THE KIND ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're afraid of right now, a test, a worry about someone's health. Don't push it away. On the in-breath, name it plainly. On the out-breath, bow to it inwardly and hand it over, asking for healing and steadiness for everyone it touches. If you pray, you can pour a little water, the way families do over the Shiva linga, and say Om Namah Shivaya; if you don't, simply wish the people in your home well.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Kapardin, the one with coiled, braided hair, the fierce Vedic god a village asked for healing.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kapardin, the braided-haired god a Vedic village asked for healing: Rudra the fierce is Shiva, the kind. Today, the last selection.

segments.voice: A little boy wants milk. He's seen another child drink it, and he asks his mother. They're poor, living in a forest hermitage, and there's no milk to give. So she stirs some flour into water and hands it to him. He drinks it, and knows it isn't milk. That small kitchen moment is where the Mahabharata begins the story of Upamanyu, the sage who handed Krishna Shiva's names.
screen: `A BOY ASKS FOR MILK.` → `FLOUR IN WATER.` → `WHERE THE NAMES CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, Upamanyu tells Krishna his own story. When the boy cries over the flour and water, his mother tells him they have nothing, and that only Shiva can give what he's asking for. So the boy sets out to worship Shiva, with his whole small life, in hard austerities. One day a visitor arrives: Indra, king of the gods, riding his white elephant, offering the boy any gift he wants. Upamanyu turns him down. He wants nothing that doesn't come from Shiva. Then the visitor changes. It was Shiva all along, testing him, and now Shiva shows himself, with Parvati beside him, and gives the boy far more than milk. Years later, when Upamanyu has taught Krishna the names, Krishna worships Shiva, and Shiva and Parvati appear to him too, and grant his wish for a son. Notice what the story allows. The boy began by asking for milk, Krishna came asking for a son, and neither is scolded. Hindus pray for things all the time: a recovery, an exam, a safe trip. But the story turns on Upamanyu's no. Offered anything by the king of the gods, he wants what comes from Shiva, and then, more than the gift, Shiva himself. That runs all through bhakti, loving devotion: you may come to God for a cup of milk, and stay for God. Across these days, a handful of names: Sthanu, Shankara, Pashupati, Nilakantha, Kapardin, and Vishnu's lotuses at every one. One more name gathers them up: Mahadeva, the great god. Not great like a king who keeps his distance. Great like the one who turned up at a poor boy's hermitage, and answered him.
screen: `UPAMANYU REFUSES INDRA'S GIFTS.` · `SHIVA REVEALS HIMSELF.` · `ASKING IS ALLOWED.` · `BHAKTI WANTS THE GOD, NOT THE GIFT.` · then, large: `MAHADEVA.`

segments.voice: Let the names you've met pass through your mind, one per breath, like beads on a string: Sthanu, steady; Shankara, well-being; Pashupati, the loosened rope; Nilakantha, the held poison; Kapardin, the healer; Mahadeva. Notice which one you linger on; that's the one that's yours for now. If you pray, say that name a few times, slowly, asking for nothing; if you don't, just rest with the word.

segments.voice: A rock on a mountainside in Kashmir. That's where this story says a teaching was waiting. Tradition remembers a teacher named Vasugupta, a devotee of Shiva, who had a dream. In it, Shiva told him that on a certain mountain there was a great stone, and on the stone, words were cut: short lines of teaching that had been forgotten. Vasugupta woke up. And now he has to decide what a dream is worth.
screen: `A ROCK IN KASHMIR.` → `VASUGUPTA'S DREAM.` → `THE SHIVA SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Vasugupta went. He climbed to the place from the dream, found the stone and touched it, and it turned over, showing the lines carved underneath. Some commentators tell it differently: Shiva taught him in the dream itself. Either way, the tradition treats the Shiva Sutras as given, not invented. This is the opening of Kashmir Shaivism. A sutra is a thread, a line so short a teacher has to unpack it. And the very first thread of this book is two words: chaitanyam atma. Consciousness is the self. Sit with how strange and how simple that is. It doesn't say you have consciousness, the way you have a phone or a cold. It says you are it. Not the body, not the name, not the job title, not the mood you woke up in. Those come and go. The awareness that notices them coming and going: that's the self. And Kashmir Shaivism takes one more step. That consciousness isn't a small private light in each head. It's Shiva's own, one consciousness, appearing as everything and everyone. So the first line of the book is also a line about God. Hindus call the self atman; this book says the atman is awareness itself, and that awareness is Shiva. Commentators in this tradition, like Kshemaraja, linger over these two words, and read the rest of the book as unfolding from them. The names pointed out at Shiva. This thread points in, at whoever is listening.
screen: `THE STONE TURNS OVER.` · `SUTRA: A THREAD TO UNPACK.` · `CHAITANYAM ATMA.` · `ONE CONSCIOUSNESS, SHIVA'S OWN.` · then, large: `CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Let sounds come in, a car, a fan, your own breathing, and thoughts too, and each time something appears, say softly to yourself: noticed. Every so often, turn around and ask what is doing the noticing, and without answering in words, rest in whatever is aware for a breath or two. If you pray, you can hold the first sutra, consciousness is the self, as your line.

1140.title: Knowing that binds
1140.hook: the second Shiva Sutra says knowledge is bondage, and a lover who goes unrecognized shows why
1140.carry: knowledge binds when it says i am only this
1140.tomorrow: why would wonder be a sign of the path?

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir Shaivism opening: a rock turned over, and the first thread of the Shiva Sutras said consciousness is the self. Today, the second thread.
screen: `CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE SELF.` · `THE SECOND THREAD.`

segments.voice: Knowledge is bondage. That's the whole second line of the Shiva Sutras, two words in Sanskrit: jnanam bandhah. Read it cold and it sounds like an attack on school, on books, on curiosity, on everything a library stands for. It isn't. But it's meant to stop you, the way a do-not-enter sign makes you look twice at the door. The first thread said consciousness is the self. This one says what goes wrong.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE IS BONDAGE.` → `NOT AN ATTACK ON BOOKS.` → `WHAT GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Consciousness is the self, and in this tradition that consciousness is Shiva's own: wide, free, whole. So why does a person feel so small? The second thread answers: knowing binds. Commentators read knowledge here as limited knowing: the quiet, constant sense of I am only this. Only this body, this anxious person, this bad grade. Not wrong information, but too small a picture of who's doing the knowing. Kshemaraja's commentary ties it to the tradition's impurities, starting with anava mala, the stain of smallness. Then a later teacher of the same Kashmir tradition, Utpaladeva, tells a little story to show the way out. A young woman has fallen in love with a man she has only heard about. She longs for him. One day he's standing right in front of her, and she feels nothing, because she doesn't know it's him. Then someone tells her: that's him. Nothing about him changes. But now her joy is complete. That, Utpaladeva says, is how it is with us and the Lord. Shiva is already here, as our own awareness, and the small knowing keeps us from seeing it. So freedom isn't getting something new. It's recognition, pratyabhijna, a word that gives a whole school in Kashmir its name. On an ordinary day, the small knowing sounds like I'm just bad at this, or I always mess up. A label that started as information and became a wall. The second thread doesn't ask you to stop knowing things. It asks who you think is doing the knowing.
screen: `JNANAM BANDHAH: KNOWING BINDS.` · `I AM ONLY THIS.` · `THE LOVER, NOT YET RECOGNIZED.` · `THAT'S HIM.` · then, large: `FREEDOM IS RECOGNITION.`

segments.voice: Let a sentence come up that starts with I'm just, or I'm only, or I always, something you say about yourself, and hold it gently. On each out-breath, let the space around it grow wider, the way the woman's whole view changed when she knew who was standing there; the label can stay, it just isn't the whole room anymore. If you pray, you can say softly: you were here all along. If you don't, rest in the first thread, consciousness is the self.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir Shaivism opening gave the second thread: knowledge is bondage, the small knowing that says I am only this. Today, a thread of wonder.
screen: `KNOWING BINDS.` · `A THREAD OF WONDER.`

segments.voice: A woman walks out of her house in Kashmir, about seven hundred years ago, and doesn't go back. Tradition remembers her as Lalla, or Lal Ded, Grandmother Lal. The stories say her married life was hard, and that she left to follow a teacher of Shiva and wander as a yogini, singing. Her short Kashmiri sayings, called vakhs, are still on people's lips there. And one of them tells how all her searching ended.
screen: `KASHMIR, 700 YEARS AGO.` → `LALLA LEAVES HOME.` → `HOW THE SEARCH ENDED.`

segments.voice: In that saying, as it's usually rendered, Lalla says she went out searching far and wide, and when at last she found the one she was looking for, he was in her own house. Another tells that her teacher gave her just one instruction: turn from what's outside to what's within. She took it so to heart that she began to dance. That's the feeling the Shiva Sutras name in one thread: vismayo yogabhumikah. Vismaya is wonder, astonishment, the wide-eyed surprise of seeing something as if for the first time. Yogabhumikah: the stages of yoga. Together: on this path, wonder is how you can tell you're on the way. Not pride. Not I've earned this. Something more like: oh. This was here the whole time? Go back to the first two threads. Consciousness is the self, Shiva's own. Knowing binds: the small sense of I am only this. When the small picture slips, commentators describe the yogi's response as delight, astonishment, because nothing new arrived. What was always home is finally seen. Wonder is what recognition feels like from the inside. Lalla's sayings belong to more than one family. Kashmiri Hindus call her Lal Ded and Lalleshwari; many Kashmiri Muslims love her too, and some call her Lalla Arifa, the one who knows. Their prayers are honestly different, and the shared thing is plain: God near enough to be found at home. So the week ends on one small word: oh.
screen: `LALLA SEARCHES FAR.` · `FOUND HIM AT HOME.` · `VISMAYA: WONDER, ASTONISHMENT.` · `WONDER MARKS THE STAGES OF YOGA.` · then, large: `RECOGNITION FEELS LIKE OH.`

segments.voice: Choose something right in front of you, your hand, a cup, the light on a wall, and look at it as if for the first time: its color, its edges, the fact that it's here at all; when the mind says it's just a cup, look again. Then turn the same wonder inward, on the plain fact that you're aware of anything, the thing Lalla found at home. If you pray, let that wonder be your prayer; if you don't, just stay with the oh.
